title: Form and sound (section 26)
hook: those who see me by form or seek me by sound walk the wrong road (as Müller renders the verse)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no beings freed: the Tathagata helps without the thought, I set them free. Your line: no one to free.

Outside a bookstore, a line wraps around the block. A famous writer is signing tonight. A young man near the front has waited three hours. He gets his photo, a handshake, the sound of the writer saying his name, and walks away glowing. Then a friend asks what the books are about, and he laughs. He hasn't read them. He saw the face, heard the voice, and missed the writer completely. Section twenty-six of the Diamond Sutra aims this same mistake at the Buddha himself.
screen: `A LINE AROUND THE BLOCK.` → `A FACE, A VOICE, A PHOTO.` → `HE NEVER READ THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti whether the Tathagata can be recognized by his bodily marks, the signs tradition says a great being bears. The sutra has asked this before; here it adds a sharp reason for the answer no. If the marks were enough, a wheel-turning king, a world ruler who bears the same marks, would be a Tathagata too. A body can look the part and not be the thing. Then the verse. In paraphrase: those who see me by my form, and those who follow me by my voice, have set out on a wrong road. They will not see me. Form is what the eye catches, sound what the ear catches. Both are real, and both are the outside. The second half of the verse is easy to skip. The Buddhas are to be seen from the Dharma; their body is the Dharma. And the Dharma's nature isn't something the mind can grab as an object. So the verse closes one road and points down another: you meet the Tathagata where the teaching is lived, not where the outline of a body stands. What the verse doesn't say matters too. A Buddhist temple may hold images and chanting. Read in a room like that, the verse doesn't ask anyone to tear the images down or fall silent. It asks where the looking stops. A statue can be a doorway. The mistake is to stand in the doorway admiring the frame.
screen: `ARE THE MARKS ENOUGH?` · `NOT BY FORM, NOT BY VOICE.` · `SEEN FROM THE DHARMA.` · `A DOORWAY, NOT THE ROOM.` · then, large: `NOT BY FORM OR SOUND.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something near you: a photo of someone you love, an image of the Buddha, or just a cup. Take in the form first, the shape, the colors, the edges, and let that be complete. Then, still looking, ask quietly what it is beyond its shape: the way a person laughs, or the hands that made the cup and the tea it held.
Form and sound. The eye's catch and the ear's catch: the verse in section twenty-six says the Tathagata isn't found there, but seen from the Dharma. Today's word.
Your line: not by form or sound. The face and the voice are only the outside. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists chant and study the Diamond Sutra, and some communities recite its verse on form and sound by heart; it's read alongside the images and chanting of temple life, as a reminder of what they point to.

chat.says: If the Buddha said not to see him by his form, why do temples have Buddha statues?
options: The verse asks where the looking stops; a statue can be a doorway to the Dharma, not the goal.
The verse says the Buddha's bodily marks prove who he is, so statues must show them.
The verse is only for monks; lay people are meant to see the Buddha by his form.
chat.meaning: The verse says the Tathagata is seen from the Dharma, not by form or voice; it doesn't ask anyone to tear images down.

Tathagata.meaning: the awakened one; a title the Buddha uses for himself

Subhuti.meaning: the elder who questions the Buddha in the Diamond Sutra

Dharma.meaning: the Buddha's teaching, and the truth it points to

wheel-turning king.meaning: a world ruler said to bear the same bodily marks

notes: The section 26 verse is paraphrased, not quoted: the outline cites Max Müller's rendering, but his exact wording was not verified. A Keeper may wish to supply Müller's text verbatim.

Versions differ on whether Subhuti first answers yes and is corrected (Kumarajiva's Chinese) or answers no at once (the Sanskrit Müller used); the script avoids saying which. Check the wheel-turning king (cakravartin) detail.

The second half of the verse (the Buddhas seen from the Dharma; the Dharma-body; the Dharma's nature not graspable) is absent from some Chinese versions; the script says only that the verse has it. Confirm.
Practice suggests an image of the Buddha as one option; confirm this is respectful.
